item.title: Neto double fires Chelsea past Everton but Martinez injury mars win
item.description: Chelsea beat Everton 2-0 in the Premier League on Saturday thanks to a double from Pedro Neto as the London club provisionally moved up to fourth in a game overshadowed by an injury to goalkeeper Emi Martinez.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chelsea beat Everton 2-0 in the Premier League on Saturday thanks to a double from Pedro Neto as the London club provisionally moved up to fourth in a game overshadowed by an injury to goalkeeper Emi Martinez. After a goalless but feisty first half that produced five yellow cards and several heated exchanges, Chelsea needed just 43 seconds after the restart to go 1-0 up when an unmarked Neto swept home. The game was paused for several minutes when Chelsea's Martinez was taken off on a stretcher following a collision with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite, with 21-year-old keeper Mike Penders coming on for his Premier League debut. Chelsea doubled their lead in the 90th minute when Neto pounced on a loose ball after Jordan Henderson's free kick was blocked by the wall, finding the bottom corner with a composed finish as Everton suffered their first defeat of the season.

item.title: At least 10 killed in fire at Bangladesh beach resort
item.description: At least 10 people were killed and several others injured in a fire on Saturday at a resort near Inani Beach in Cox's Bazar, a popular tourist destination in southeastern Bangladesh, officials said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: At least 10 people were killed and several others injured in a fire on Saturday at a resort near Inani Beach in Cox's Bazar, a popular tourist destination in southeastern Bangladesh, officials said. The fire broke out at a three-storey wooden resort The resort was operating without a valid fire safety licence, fire service officials said A five-member investigation committee has been formed to investigate the cause of the fire Authorities also said they would examine possible regulatory failures The incident has raised concerns about fire safety compliance at tourist resorts in the coastal district

item.title: Iran's Guards say two tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Saturday that two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Saturday that two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported. State media said both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil. There was no independent confirmation of the reports. IRNA reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use an unauthorised route through the strategic waterway. The second vessel was left immobilised after striking a mine, it added. State media earlier reported that the other tanker had also struck a mine while attempting to transit the strait via a route not authorised by Iran. The incidents come amid heightened tensions around the strait, a key oil shipping route. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway due to the US-Israeli war on Iran have boosted global energy prices and inflation. Maritime officials said on Wednesday that a container ship and a dry bulk carrier [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"sank"] near the strait after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents. [USN:L1N45U0E0 TEXT:"Attacks"] around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.

item.title: Zelenski afirma que la reunión trilateral de líderes podría celebrarse en la cumbre del G-20
item.description: El presidente ucraniano, Volodímir Zelenski afirmó el sábado que podría celebrarse una reunión trilateral entre Ucrania, Estados Unidos y Rusia durante la cumbre del G20 en Estados Unidos o en otro país.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El presidente ucraniano, Volodímir Zelenski afirmó el sábado que podría celebrarse una reunión trilateral entre Ucrania, Estados Unidos y Rusia durante la cumbre del G20 en Estados Unidos o en otro país. "La reunión podría celebrarse entonces en Estados Unidos durante la cumbre del G20. Pero aún no ha habido confirmación ni por parte de Rusia ni de Estados Unidos. También podría celebrarse en un país europeo", afirmó. La cumbre del G20 está prevista para diciembre.

item.title: Zelenskiy asked neighbours to let grain cargoes through, Hungary PM Magyar says
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has asked neighbours Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Hungary to allow the transit of Ukrainian grain cargoes because of a Black Sea blockade, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has asked neighbours Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Hungary to allow the transit of Ukrainian grain cargoes because of a Black Sea blockade, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Saturday. Magyar, who agreed with Zelenskiy to [USN:L8N4620U6 TEXT:"reset Ukraine-Hungary ties"] at talks on Friday, said he would have no objections to the measure if the Ukrainian grain cargoes only passed through Hungary to other destinations, private broadcaster RTL reported. Ukraine is among the world's top producers of wheat, corn and sunflower seeds and around 90% of its exports of such crops go through the Black Sea, where a Russian campaign of attacks has [USN:L8N44605L TEXT:"almost halted agricultural exports"] from its Black Sea ports. The grain transit would be modelled on a solution proposed shortly after Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine , Magyar said. "(Zelenskiy) asked Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary and all neighbouring countries to allow transit, as they had three or four years ago at the start of the war," Magyar told RTL in an interview. Magyar has taken a less confrontational stance towards Kyiv than Viktor Orban, whom he succeeded as Hungary's prime minister. Magyar had repeatedly said, however, that Hungary would not send arms to Ukraine and demanded progress on the rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority. Magyar also assured Zelenskiy of his full solidarity over the "inhuman Russian aggression" against Ukraine. "He mentioned to me during our one-on-one meeting that it would help them a lot if they could transport maize in sealed trains to Western Europe," Magyar said. "I said as long as it merely transits the country, there would be no obstacle." In late August the European Commission forecast the European Union's maize harvest, typically its second-largest cereals crop, would be 50.1 million metric tons this year, a near two-decade low and about a fifth below the average of the past three years. Farmers in France and Hungary were hit especially hard as record heat and drought had [USN:L8N44T097 TEXT:"decimated maize plantings"].

item.title: China central bank chief supports closer IMF surveillance of fiscal, spillover risks
item.description: China's central bank governor said on Saturday that Beijing supports the International Monetary Fund in boosting the surveillance of fiscal risks in "major advanced economies" and their spillover effects.
item.dc:creator: Selena Li
item.content:encoded: China's central bank governor said on Saturday that Beijing supports the International Monetary Fund in boosting the surveillance of fiscal risks in "major advanced economies" and their spillover effects. People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng was addressing the International Monetary and Financial Committee meeting during annual gatherings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. Surging borrowing costs, chronic high fiscal deficits in major economies, and turbulent investor sentiment, aggravated by massive capital expenditures in artificial intelligence, have triggered a widespread global [USN:L1N45N05N TEXT:"bond market rout"]. Pan urged the IMF to analyse global imbalances and place greater emphasis on the impact of financial factors such as capital flows on these imbalances, a statement from the bank showed. The central bank chief said China supports the multilateral trading system and opposes all forms of protectionist measures. Earlier this week, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said China [USN:S0N40K04E TEXT:"must pivot"] from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption.

item.title: Zelenskiy hopes for meeting with US and Russia during G20 summit
item.description: Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday. The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December. "The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelenskiy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat. He added: "This meeting could take place in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The United States has consistently mentioned the United Arab Emirates or Saudi Arabia." Zelenskiy said Ukrainian negotiators had spoken to US officials on Friday but gave no other details. He also said that Europe needed its own track for talks with Russia, with which relations are strained by Moscow's war in Ukraine . US President Donald Trump has [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"declined"] to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the more than four-year-old war, and Zelenskiy has [USN:L1N4620UE TEXT:"criticised"] Trump for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. STARLINK Zelenskiy said the Ukrainian military was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions placed on services provided by satellite company Starlink. "Today, our interceptor drones are not operating because of speed limitations," Zelenskiy said. He said Ukraine had been told that the speed restrictions had been caused by technical issues but that tests of Starlink on the territory of the European Union had shown there were no such issues there. Trump [USN:L6N462112 TEXT:"said"] on Friday he did not think either he or Elon Musk - whose company SpaceX developed the Starshield system used by Ukraine's military - was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia. The reduction in services provided by the satellite company [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"interrupted communications"] with headquarters and caused internet speeds to drop.

item.title: Gas lacrimógeno y enfrentamientos sacuden ciudades francesas en las protestas por costo de la vida
item.description: La policía lanzó gases lacrimógenos y se enfrentó a los manifestantes en varias ciudades francesas el sábado, cuando algunas de las protestas más violentas de los últimos años, motivadas por el costo de la vida y los servicios públicos, llevaron a miles de personas a las calles.
item.dc:creator: Clotaire Achi, Janis Laizans
item.content:encoded: La policía lanzó gases lacrimógenos y se enfrentó a los manifestantes en varias ciudades francesas el sábado, cuando algunas de las protestas más violentas de los últimos años, motivadas por el costo de la vida y los servicios públicos, llevaron a miles de personas a las calles. Las autoridades francesas indicaron que, a mediodía, se habían registrado 140 manifestaciones en las que participaron 32 800 personas fuera de París, y achacaron los disturbios a lo que describieron como la "ultraizquierda". Las protestas comenzaron el mes pasado en institutos de los suburbios pobres del norte de París, donde la indignación por la falta de profesores y el mal estado de las instalaciones se convirtió en un movimiento más amplio centrado en la desigualdad, el gasto público y el nivel de vida. Se registraron incidentes violentos en varias ciudades, entre ellos actos de vandalismo en Marsella y ataques dirigidos contra la policía, los medios de comunicación y edificios públicos, según informó el Ministerio del Interior. Se observó una fuerte presencia policial en el centro de París, especialmente cerca de lugares emblemáticos como los Campos Elíseos y el Arco del Triunfo, que quedaron excluidos de los recorridos de las dos manifestaciones autorizadas. Los manifestants, ataviados con chalecos de alta visibilidad, bloquearon las calles, lo que recordó al movimiento de los "chalecos amarillos" que marcó el anterior mandato del presidente Emmanuel Macron. En Marsella, el alcalde afirmó que el ayuntamiento había sido objeto de actos de vandalismo y que se estaban enviando refuerzos policiales a la ciudad tras las conversaciones mantenidas con el primer ministro y el ministro del Interior. "Luchamos porque el costo de la vida es demasiado elevado, porque el precio del combustible es demasiado alto, porque los alumnos de secundaria están siendo atacados violentamente y resultando heridos por todo el país solo por intentar manifestarse y pedir más profesores y unas condiciones de aprendizaje dignas", afirmó Lola, una manifestante de 19 años en París. Macron, que el viernes instó a la calma, entra en la recta final de su presidencia en medio de un panorama político fragmentado y una presión creciente sobre la economía. Los esfuerzos de Francia por reducir la deuda pública no han logrado tranquilizar a los inversionistas, lo que ha llevado los costos de financiación del Estado a sus niveles más altos en más de dos décadas. RESPUESTA POLICIAL BAJO ESCRUTINIO Las tácticas policiales han suscitado críticas tras una serie de heridos entre los manifestantes, entre ellos un adolescente que perdió una mano tras recoger una granada aturdidora. El primer ministro, Sébastien Lecornu, afirmó que también habían resultado heridos más de 900 agentes de policía. El organismo de control policial está investigando al menos dos docenas de denuncias de violencia policial. Francia suspendió el uso de granadas aturdidoras durante las manifestaciones estudiantiles, pero el ministro del Interior, Laurent Núñez, afirmó que podrían utilizarse el sábado. Las convocatorias en las redes sociales para que los veteranos de movimientos de protesta anteriores se unieran a las manifestaciones parecen haber ampliado la participación, lo que aumenta la posibilidad de que estas alcancen una mayor envergadura. El movimiento de los Chalecos Amarillos surgió en 2018 en oposición a los impuestos sobre el diésel, antes de ampliarse a una protesta más general contra el costo de la vida y la desigualdad.

item.title: Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'
item.description: Ukraine on Saturday rejected Russia's claim to have captured more than 1,800 square km (695 square miles) of territory and nearly 100 settlements, including the eastern town of Dobropillia, since September 1.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine on Saturday rejected Russia's claim to have captured more than 1,800 square km (695 square miles) of territory and nearly 100 settlements, including the eastern town of [USN:L1N4620VZ TEXT:"Dobropillia"], since September 1. On Friday, the chief of Russia's General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, told President Vladimir Putin that Russian forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements and made significant territorial gains since the start of last month. Ukraine's General Staff spokesman Andriy Kovaliov dismissed the claims as false. "In fact, through their active operations, the Ukrainian Defence Forces have liberated more territory since the beginning of autumn than the enemy has managed to capture," he said in an emailed statement. "The Russian military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its political leadership and domestic audience," he said. Russia's advances along the front line have slowed this year but its forces have been bearing down on the so-called "fortress belt" cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the capture of which would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire industrialised Donetsk region. Kovaliov also rejected Gerasimov's claims that Russian troops had reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk and were advancing in the suburbs of Sloviansk. He said Dobropillia, southwest of the two cities, remained under Ukrainian control despite sustained Russian attacks. Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield claims. With many front lines largely static across a deadly "kill zone" , both sides have intensified their air campaigns. Russia [USN:L8N44V0TY TEXT:"fired "]hundreds of ballistic missiles over the summer and early autumn and is widely expected to target critical infrastructure including heating and power sites into the winter. Ukraine, which has a far smaller missile arsenal, has launched hundreds of long-range drone attacks on Russian refineries, ships and warehouses.

item.title: South Africa still mulling over permutations for second test against Australia
item.description: One thing that looks certain is a return to the team for fast bowler Kagiso Rabada.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Africa have not yet confirmed their playing XI for the second test against Australia which starts in Gqeberha on Sunday as they assess the likely impact of the weather on the game and consider playing two spinners again. The home side were beaten by 214 runs in the first test of the three-match series in Durban and need to improve with both bat and ball as they seek put pressure on the tourists. Captain Temba Bavuma confirmed on Saturday that the team were still mulling over several options for their playing personnel. “We would like to see what happens tomorrow,” he told reporters. “Whether we go with two spinners is probably one of the biggest considerations. “Whether we go with one spinner, whether we play an all-rounder and which all-rounder that is, it all comes down to the balance of the team. Those are the dynamics we have to consider.” One thing that looks certain is a return to the team for fast bowler Kagiso Rabada, who has been cleared to play after missing the first test with a hamstring injury. “He has been released by the fitness team and is available for selection. He will obviously be a big addition and a boost to the team on the field. He is raring to go,” Bavuma said. “The bowlers feed massively off him. He leads the attack in everything that he does and brings an extra level of confidence to the unit. Whether he is on the field or off the field, there is always a benefit. “Any captain would be happy to have a guy like KG in his bowling attack, so that brings a big smile to my face.” Bavuma said his side needed to improve with the bat to challenge Australia. “We need to be much more ruthless in how we execute and, more importantly, when the opportunity is there, we need to go on and do something big for the team,” he said. “We can take the little good moments that we had with the bat (in the first test) and build on those.”

item.title: Zelensky dénonce de nouvelles restrictions imposées par Starlink
item.description: L'Ukraine n'est pas en mesure d'utiliser ses systèmes d'interception contre les attaques de drones russes en raison de restrictions de vitesse imposées par Starlink, a déclaré samedi le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, ajoutant que Kyiv discutait de cette question avec des responsables américains.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Ukraine n'est pas en mesure d'utiliser ses systèmes d'interception contre les attaques de drones russes en raison de restrictions de vitesse imposées par Starlink, a déclaré samedi le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, ajoutant que Kyiv discutait de cette question avec des responsables américains. Dans une conversation organisée sur la messagerie Whatsapp avec des journalistes, Volodimir Zelensky a dit s'être vu répondre que ces restrictions étaient dues à des problèmes techniques. Le chef de l'Etat ukrainien a ajouté qu'il avait testé le réseau satellitaire dirigé par Elon Musk sur le territoire de l'Union européenne et qu'il n'y avait pas rencontré de tels problèmes, le système fonctionnant à des vitesses élevées. Volodimir Zelensky a également déclaré que des négociateurs de paix ukrainiens et américains pourraient se rencontrer la semaine prochaine. Il a précisé que les négociateurs ukrainiens avaient parlé vendredi avec la délégation américaine, sans donner de détails. Le président ukrainien a aussi évoqué la possibilité d'une rencontre trilatérale entre l'Ukraine, les Etats-Unis et la Russie en marge d'un sommet du G20 à Miami en décembre, tout en ajoutant que ni Washington et Moscou n'avaient confirmé la tenue d'une telle rencontre et que d'autres lieux étaient envisageables. Le G20 réunit les vingt principales économies mondiales dont les Etats-Unis et la Russie. L'Ukraine n'en fait pas partie. "La rencontre pourrait avoir lieu aux Etats-Unis, lors du sommet du G20. Mais il n'y a pour l'instant aucune confirmation, ni de la part de la Russie, ni de celle des Etats-Unis. Elle pourrait également se tenir dans un pays européen", a indiqué Volodimir Zelensky.

item.title: Papa León sale del hospital el sábado tras una operación de cáncer de pulmón
item.description: El papa León salió del hospital de Roma el sábado por la tarde para regresar al Vaticano tras someterse a una intervención quirúrgica por cáncer de pulmón hace cuatro días.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: El papa León salió del hospital de Roma el sábado por la tarde para regresar al Vaticano tras someterse a una intervención quirúrgica por cáncer de pulmón hace cuatro días. El pontífice, de 71 años, caminó sin ayuda hasta el coche que le esperaba, deteniéndose para hablar con quienes le deseaban una pronta recuperación a la salida del Hospital Gemelli de Roma. Sus médicos habían indicado anteriormente que se encontraba lo suficientemente bien como para volver a casa tras realizarle los últimos análisis de sangre y pruebas de imagen torácicas. El papa, que el martes se sometió a una operación para extirparle el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho, tendrá su primer acto público desde la intervención el domingo, cuando dirija las oraciones semanales con los peregrinos en la Plaza de San Pedro al mediodía (1000 GMT). A León le han diagnosticado un adenocarcinoma de pulmón, el tipo más común de cáncer de pulmón. El diagnóstico, en el caso de un papa conocido por ser relativamente joven y enérgico y que fue elegido apenas en mayo de 2025, causó conmoción y suscitó interrogantes sobre cómo se desarrollará su papado a medida que afronte la enfermedad. Los médicos del papa han afirmado que la intervención quirúrgica se ha desarrollado con éxito y sin complicaciones. Aún no han revelado el tamaño del tumor ni si la enfermedad se había extendido a los ganglios linfáticos cercanos, factores clave para determinar el pronóstico.

item.title: Vaste manifestation à Tunis contre le président Saïed
item.description: Des milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi à Tunis contre le président Kaïs Saïed, l'accusant de saper la démocratie et l'économie du pays.
item.dc:creator: Tarek Amara
item.content:encoded: Des milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi à Tunis contre le président Kaïs Saïed, l'accusant de saper la démocratie et l'économie du pays. La manifestation, l'une des plus importantes de ces dernières années, organisée à l'appel de la puissance Union générale tunisienne du travail, principale centrale syndicale du pays, et des organisations de la société civile, s'inscrit dans un contexte de crise économique, de dégradation des services publics, de coupures récurrentes d'eau et d'électricité et de pénuries de médicaments et de biens essentiels. Dans une rare démonstration d'unité, des représentants de nombreux partis d'opposition ont rejoint avocats, médecins, journalistes, chômeurs dans le cortège défilant sur l'avenue Habib-Bourguiba, dans le centre de la capitale tunisienne. Des centaines de policiers en tenue anti-émeute ont été déployés. "Nous n'avons pas peur, le pouvoir appartient au peuple", ou "Les prisons sont pleines, les gens ont faim", ont notamment scandé les manifestants. "Ça suffit. Le pays est en train de s'effondrer. Nous subissons une crise après l'autre", a expliqué Yassine Gharseli, venu spécialement de Sfax, à 250 km au sud de la capitale. "Je ne suis pas prêt à lâcher, même si je suis la dernière voix dans ce pays", a-t-il dit. Le président Kaïs Saïed a dissous le Parlement tunisien en 2021 et s'est arrogé de vastes pouvoirs, gouvernant par décrets, dans ce que ses opposants qualifient de coup d'Etat.

item.title: Albanian anti-government protesters clash with police in Tirana
item.description: Thousands of young Albanians gathered outside the Education Ministry in the centre of the capital Tirana on Saturday on the fifth day of a growing student-led movement to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Thousands of young Albanians gathered outside the Education Ministry in the centre of the capital Tirana on Saturday on the fifth day of a growing [USN:L6N4620YF TEXT:"student-led movement"] to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protest turned violent when a group of young people wearing masks hurled rocks at riot police, who responded with stun grenades, tear gas and a water cannon. Demonstrations over corruption and a lack of jobs have begun spreading throughout Albania. In Tirana this week, protesters smashed windows, set alight government buildings and clashed with police. Police figures showed that 500 protesters had been detained so far, 330 of whom were released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters were registered as injured, although many injuries to protesters are likely to have gone unrecorded. The unrest is emerging as the biggest threat to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in elections last year. It follows months of largely peaceful protests triggered by plans to build a [USN:L1N42H07R TEXT:"luxury resort"]on Albania's pristine southern coastline, backed by investors including US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land had been wrongfully sold for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. Rama's administration has been dogged by corruption scandals and analysts say Albania is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU. Rama, who denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and would protect their right to protest. "My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect our citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward — together with this governing majority, which holds a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030," he said on Facebook. Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the accession process among Balkan countries. Albania's unrest coincides with growing street protests elsewhere in Europe. In France, high-school students have been [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"protesting"] for weeks to demand more teachers and better facilities, a campaign that looks to be spreading to other population groups. Spain this month experienced broad protests against high rents and a lack of housing, which prompted the government to call a [USN:L8N46011N TEXT:"snap election"].

item.title: Davidovich Fokina beats Zverev, sets up all-Spanish Shanghai final with Jodar
item.description: Davidovich Fokina, the 25th seed, fired 36 winners in the two-hour, two-minute contest to secure only his second victory over Zverev in eight meetings.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina upset top seed Alexander Zverev 5-7 6-4 6-3 on Saturday to reach the Shanghai Masters final, where he was joined by fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar after the 20-year-old sensation downed former world number one Daniil Medvedev. Davidovich Fokina, the 25th seed, fired 36 winners in the two-hour, two-minute contest to secure only his second victory over Zverev in eight meetings. His previous win against the German came in the round of 32 at the Canadian Open in 2023. He earned his first break of the match to take the second set, forcing a decider with a stunning backhand passing shot on the run that capped a bruising baseline exchange and brought the crowd to their feet. Carrying that momentum into the final set, Davidovich Fokina broke Zverev for a 2-0 lead and never relinquished control, booking a place in the second ATP Masters 1000 final of his career after finishing runner-up in Monte Carlo in 2022. Landing 82% of his first serves and repeatedly exposing Zverev on the forehand side, the 27-year-old secured one of the biggest victories of his career. "I knew that if I stayed there all match, I could get at least one chance and I took it there in the second set," Davidovich Fokina said. "Then in the third set, I think I was better physically. The early break in the third set gave me a lot of power. "I focused on just playing, not mattering about the result but enjoying." Davidovich Fokina has now won nine consecutive matches in China after lifting his second tour-level title at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu last month. It was a disappointing end to the week for Zverev, a seven-time ATP Masters 1000 champion whose best result in Shanghai remains his runner-up finish to Medvedev in 2019. The 29-year-old has otherwise enjoyed a fine season, ending his Grand Slam drought at the [USN:L1N42F08C TEXT:"French Open"] before claiming a second major title at the [USN:L6N4550DD TEXT:"US Open"] and securing the ATP [USN:L1N45Y0DG TEXT:"year-end world number one"] ranking after Jannik [USN:L1N45S0CV TEXT:"Sinner was sidelined"] for the remainder of the season with a knee injury. Twelfth seed Jodar continued his remarkable rise by becoming the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history and strengthening his chances of qualifying for the ATP Finals in his first full season on the tour with a 6-3 6-4 victory over fifth-seeded Russian Medvedev. The aggressive right-hander, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, is seeking the second ATP title of his career after capturing his maiden crown in Morocco and will now compete in his first Masters 1000 final. "It was a very tough match," Jodar said. "In the first set all the games were very close, with breakpoints for him, breakpoints for me. "I'm super happy with how I handled the important moments in the first set, and also how I returned and served. "Daniil is always a very tough player. I think he played great today. So I had to be at my best level to beat him." Sunday's championship match will mark the first meeting between Jodar and Davidovich Fokina.

item.title: Tunisians stage biggest protest in years against President Saied
item.description: Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years in the capital on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule.
item.dc:creator: Tarek Amara
item.content:encoded: Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years in the capital on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and [USN:L1N4610HN TEXT:"mishandling the economy"] in a growing challenge to his rule. The demonstration, led by the major UGTT labour union and civil society groups, comes as Tunisia grapples with an economic crisis, worsening public services, recurring water and power cuts, and shortages of medicines and essential goods. Saied seized broad powers in 2021 and 2022, dissolving parliament, dismissing dozens of judges and ruling by decree, moves that opponents described as a coup. Rights groups say he has intensified a crackdown on civil society, journalists and opposition figures. Saied rejects those allegations, saying he is not a dictator, and has accused his opponents of engineering economic crises to fuel social unrest. In a rare show of unity, opposition parties from across the political spectrum joined lawyers, [USN:L8N3WU2C1 TEXT:"doctors"], journalists, unemployed people and civil society groups in marching along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a focal point of the 2011 protests that helped trigger the Arab Spring uprisings. The protest poses a significant challenge to Saied after years of divisions weakened the opposition's ability to mobilise large crowds. "Silence will no longer be acceptable ... the state cannot built by concentrating all powers in the hand of one person", Slah Eddine Salmi, head of the UGTT, told the rally. Hundreds of police were deployed across the capital. Protesters chanted: "No fear, power belongs to the people!" and "The prisons are full, people are hungry!". They also revived the iconic slogan of the 2011 uprising, which in Tunisia was notably peaceful: "The people want the fall of the regime!" They called for the release of Saied's [USN:L8N40A021 TEXT:"critics"] and demanded an end to what they described as attacks on trade union rights. Some carried banners expressing frustration over unemployment and [USN:L6N3W001W TEXT:"pollution."] "Enough is enough! The country is collapsing. We suffer from power and water cuts, and one crisis after another," said Yassine Gharseli, a protester from Sfax, about 250 km (155 miles) south of Tunis. "I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom and I'm not about to give up, even if I become the last voice in the country."

item.title: India's food regulator proposes ban on added sugars in infant foods
item.description: India's food safety regulator on Saturday proposed a ban on adding sucrose and fructose to food products for infants up to six months of age, tightening rules on added sugars in infant nutrition products.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India's food safety regulator on Saturday proposed a ban on adding sucrose and fructose to food products for infants up to six months of age, tightening rules on added sugars in infant nutrition products. Under existing rules, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred carbohydrate sources in infant nutrition products, while sucrose and fructose can be added when required, subject to prescribed limits, the regulator said. The move comes amid an intensifying [USN:L1N463039 TEXT:"food safety crackdown"] in India, where regulators have forced local eateries and branded restaurants to suspend operations, while a push for front-of-pack [USN:L1N45K079 TEXT:"warning labels"] has rattled the country's more than $100 billion packaged food industry. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said the proposed measure aims to reduce infants' exposure to added sugars and address health risks linked to childhood obesity. The existing regulations set nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for infant nutrition products intended for children from birth to 24 months of age, it said. Activists and officials have long raised concerns about rising obesity rates, particularly among children. India had 180 million overweight or obese adults in 2021, a figure projected to reach 450 million by 2050, according to a study published in the medical journal The Lancet. The FSSAI and some state regulators have intensified checks on food safety in recent months, releasing regular public updates including photos and videos of raids that have drawn widespread attention online. In August, the [USN:L6N46302P TEXT:"FSSAI proposed"] a red hexagonal stamp on labels of food products high in any two or more nutrients of concern such as sugar, salt or saturated fat, but tightened the proposal after a public outcry, saying a warning would now be required if even one nutrient exceeds the prescribed level.

item.title: Egypt's Sisi says his presidency will end in 2030, outlines plan to prepare future leaders
item.description: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray
item.content:encoded: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then. The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general, the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs. Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme. Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed". He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts. "I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said. The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament. [USN:L5N3GA3X9 TEXT:"Sisi"], 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030. The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood — Egypt's first democratically elected leader — following mass protests. He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.

item.title: India's ICICI Bank Q2 profit rises 20.1%, beats estimates
item.description: Indian private lender ICICI Bank reported a higher-than-expected profit for its second quarter on Saturday, driven by stronger loan demand and lower provisions for bad loans.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: Indian private lender ICICI Bank (ICBK.NS) reported a higher-than-expected profit for its second quarter on Saturday, driven by stronger loan demand and lower provisions for bad loans. The country's second-largest private lender by market capitalisation posted a standalone net profit of 148.43 billion Indian rupees ($1.56 billion) for the three months ended September, compared with 123.59 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts had expected a profit of 142.51 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG. Indian lenders have seen strong loan growth during the quarter across both corporate and retail segments. ICICI Bank's net interest income rose 17.7% to 253.39 billion rupees, aided by a 30% increase in total loans. Deposits grew 27.1% from a year earlier. Its net interest margin, a key measure of profitability, narrowed to 4.18% from 4.36% in the previous quarter. Funds kept aside for potential bad loans and other losses fell 6.9% to 8.51 billion rupees. The bank's other income, which includes income from bonds and other investments, rose 6.2% to 80.47 billion rupees amid volatile currency and debt markets. The lender's asset quality improved, with the gross non-performing asset ratio at 1.20% at the end of September, compared with 1.38% in the prior three months. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: Chuck Lorre on his reign as the ‘King of Sitcoms’
item.description: Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift. Lorre knows something about making it happen. Dubbed the “King of Sitcoms,” he has spent decades making audiences laugh, from his early work as a writer on the hit comedy “Roseanne” to creating shows, including “The Big Bang Theory,” “Two and a Half Men,” “Mom,” and “Mike & Molly.” In his newly released memoir, “Sitcom,” Lorre turns that comic instinct on his own life, writing candidly about his missteps, while also looking back at the television successes and creative battles that shaped his career. Speaking with Reuters from Los Angeles, he discusses why character is key to great comedy, what he learned from getting things wrong, and why he’s optimistic about the TV industry’s future. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The memoir is very funny despite tackling difficult subjects, from failed marriages to addiction and Scientology. What made you want to open up about them now? From the outset, I was trying to write it as if I was having a conversation with somebody. Rather than reporting or reiterating stuff, I was trying to write it as if I was talking to the audience or talking to a person; more conversational as opposed to you know, being locked up in the prose of it all. I've been talking about these crazy chapters of my life for a long time and dear friend nudged me for at least two years to start writing it down. And once I started writing it down, I was quite pleasantly surprised. I realized it was cathartic. It was it was a little bit of therapy for me. Having finished the darned thing, what became really clear was all the missteps I've made in my life were all necessary for me to arrive at where I am, and I am deeply grateful for where I am. So the path may have been bumpy, but that's what was required. What most excites you about television right now, and what terrifies you? There's plenty in this world that is terrifying, but I wouldn't put TV in that category. Actually, I'm an optimist about how the business is changing. I've heard people complain that there's too many choices. And to me that's like, really? Does that mean when you walk into a supermarket, you complain that there's too many choices? That's got to be a good thing. When I came up in this in television, there was three and a half networks. Fox was just starting. And that was it. If those three said no, it's simply not going to happen. Now there's I don't know how many platforms capable of helping a writer (or) performer create something and perhaps get it seen by a legitimate audience. Of all the shows you’ve created, which felt most miraculous? Probably Big Bang. I mean, the first pilot was an abject failure, with the exception of (co-stars) Johnny Galecki and Jim Parsons. I had to wrap my head around the fact that it was poorly written and, when we were given another opportunity one year later, we got a chance to write a better pilot. You don't get do-overs in this business, but we did. I didn't understand what we were creating till we created it. I didn't understand how viscerally the audience was going to connect with these outliers, these brilliant but incompetent characters. What makes a great comedy? It's really very simple. It's about characters. Well-designed, thought out characters, portrayed by the right actor. I adored "Cheers" and "Seinfeld" and "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Archie Bunker," Norman Lear's stuff. I wasn't watching for the plot. The storytelling of it was secondary. It was these extraordinary characters that I loved and I wanted to see them every week. And that's how I've always approached creating television shows. Character, character, character. I don't think I could sit here and remember one storyline for "Cheers," but I never missed an episode because I wanted to see those characters. Those characters made me laugh. And I think that's the secret sauce for comedy. Obviously, when you work in the drama world, plotting is an entirely different thing. You're watching for the adventure, the hero's journey. That's a story. But even in that world, which I know very little about, I'm thinking about character. Going back to the importance of casting, you write about the resistance you faced casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly,” with one network executive pushing for a slimmer actress. How much has the industry changed, and how did you learn which battles were worth fighting? Well, the good news is, because I've had some success, I don't have that many battles anymore. But it took a long time for me to fight for who I believed in as opposed to being a good soldier and taking direction. I learned the hard way that when you do what you're told to do by others and you fail, it's your failure. It's not theirs. At a certain point, I started to dig my heels in and I think first and most formidably (was) with Jon Cryer. I talk about how much resistance I got from CBS to cast Jon in "Two and a Half Men" and then Melissa McCarthy. Here was a generational talent and it was "over my dead body" kind of casting. And I went, "Fine, well, produce a dead body because we're going over it." I guess what I'm trying to say is, it took me a while to find the courage to fight these fights. I didn't have it in the beginning. I was too frightened about being tossed aside and sent home. How concerned are you about AI in the writers’ room? Are the protections won in the 2023 writers’ strike enough? There's plenty of reason to be concerned about this technology. Television would be the least of it, I would think. Why is that? I just think, if we're going to prioritize our concerns, for me AI is concerning in that it could topple civilization, not take away jobs on sitcoms, not that that's not important. But creating an intelligence that so wildly surpasses human intelligence is an incredibly risky endeavor. Look what we've done as the apex predator on this planet. Imagine what would happen if there was an apex-apex predator that viewed us the way we view insects. That scares me. Do you expect to see more shows tapping into those fears? We did an episode on "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" with an AI overlord that has shock collars around everyone so when they get angry or contentious and asocial, they're shocked into submission. You write that good TV writing starts with reading good writing. What happens to television if people are reading less? I really love words. I love the meaning of words, the sound of words, the music of words. And comedy, from my perspective, is really absolutely correct use of words to cause a response; to cause laughter. And laughter happens to you. Real laughter is involuntary. It should surprise the laugher. And that's a result of both words and images. I guess I could be concerned about a future where words become less relevant because they're my favorite things. Finally, some quick-fire questions. If you had to cast someone to portray you, who would you insist on? Idris Elba. No? Maybe not. (laughs) Why would you even ask that question? Are we going to make a movie out of the book? You never know! If you could revisit one of your shows, which would it be? "Dharma and Greg." I've always felt a profound regret for having left. There was so much more to explore, but I didn't know how. What’s your comfort watch? I really am drawn to dramas. I like to watch what I don't do. I love "Slow Horses" and "Furious." "Lucky" was another thing I saw and really enjoyed. "The Diplomat" is (also) terrific. As far as current comedies are concerned, if I want to laugh, I watch John Oliver and Jon Stewart. They absolutely know how to make me laugh out loud. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Egypte Sissi assure que sa présidence prendra fin en 2030
item.description: Le président égyptien Abdel Fattah al Sissi a assuré samedi que son mandat à la tête de l'Etat prendrait fin comme prévu en 2030.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le président égyptien Abdel Fattah al Sissi a assuré samedi que son mandat à la tête de l'Etat prendrait fin comme prévu en 2030. Au pouvoir depuis le coup d'Etat militaire en 2013 qui a renversé le président islamiste Mohamed Morsi élu un an plus tôt, l'ancien chef de l'armée a déclaré que la question de son départ était "entièrement tranchée". "J'ai dit que la Constitution égyptienne ne serait pas modifiée", a déclaré Abdel Fattah al Sissi lors d'une cérémonie de remise des diplômes à l'Académie militaire égyptienne. "C'est une question entièrement tranchée qui ne sera pas discutée." Le président égyptien, qui est âgé de 71 ans, effectue un mandat de six ans depuis sa réélection en 2024. Des amendements constitutionnels approuvés par référendum en 2019 ont prolongé de quatre à six ans la durée du mandat présidentiel et autorisé Abdel Fattah al Sissi à solliciter un troisième mandat.

item.title: Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
item.description: Friction has centered on James Blair, chief of Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. "What's really happening is a circular firing squad," a source said.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Bo Erickson, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm strategy"], questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions. Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races. Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation. As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said. "What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said. Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration. Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterization, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment. TRUMP HAS LONG DISTANCED HIMSELF FROM POLITICAL SETBACKS Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections. But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war. Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections. Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!" Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said. One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers. For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said. In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same." In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year. Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a fight is not worth responding to." $200 MILLION AND REDISTRICTING With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at $200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said. Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said. Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state's congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage. "The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said. Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one of them said. It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term. Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

item.title: Exotic species appear off California thanks to an unusually strong El Niño
item.description: The longfin bigeye fish was spotted in California for the first time last month, and the first sea turtles of any kind nested on California beaches. Meanwhile, a venomous yellow-bellied sea snake swam ashore as whale sharks and hammerheads cruised just off the coast.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Trotta, Matt Silverstein
item.content:encoded: The longfin bigeye fish was spotted in California for the first time last month, and the first sea turtles of any kind nested on California beaches. Meanwhile, a venomous yellow-bellied sea snake swam ashore as whale sharks and hammerheads cruised just off the coast. Exotic species have been visiting California's shores since an unusually strong El Niño weather phenomenon arrived this year. Occurring naturally every few years, El Niño brings warm ocean water farther north, and tropical species with it, providing California with a stunning visual display that has become ever more evident with the advent of drone and video technology. "There's kind of a buzz. Fishermen are loving it for sure. I'm as interested as anybody else. It's strange times," said Nate Jaros, vice president of animal care at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach. Other visitors include flying fish and manta rays. California had already experienced an unusual marine heat wave just before its arrival. This year's phenomenon coincided with a string of hurricanes in the eastern Pacific, fueling sea level rise and large waves that have [USN:L6N45D11J TEXT:"destroyed homes and denuded some Southern California beaches"] of sand. Preparing for more effects to come this winter, California has declared a state of emergency. But it has provided a bounty for businesses like Dana Wharf Sportfishing & Whale Watching. Co-owner Donna Kalez said anglers have pulled in 5,000 yellowfin tuna this year, compared to 2 a year ago. They are also landing wahoo and dorado, also known as mahi-mahi, a green fish with a blunt head giving it the profile of a bulldozer. "Dorado is very exciting because they're very acrobatic, so they jump out of the water. We catch them off kelp paddies, and it's a thrill," Kalez said. Experts expect conditions to mostly return to normal after El Niño, a natural phenomenon predating human-caused climate change, passes next year. The greatest short-term harm may be to kelp, which thrives in colder waters and provides habitat for multiple species, experts say. "It’s good for some sharks and probably bad for others," said Chris Lowe, director of the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach. "For animals that can't move, that's a bigger problem, right? Most sharks that are highly mobile. They can simply move." The yellow-bellied sea snake may have venomous fangs but cannot swim like a large shark. When an apparently sick one swam ashore in Orange County in September, a beachgoer used a palm frond to lift it off the sand and drop it in the sea. Jaros said that based on cellphone video he had little doubt it was the yellow-bellied sea snake, Hydrophis platurus. There have only been six or seven confirmed sightings in California, said William Ludt, associate curator of ichthyology at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. The last confirmed sighting came during the El Niño of 2015-2016, he said. Exotic sharks such as the whale shark — a gentle giant and the largest fish on Earth — and the more menacing-looking hammerheads venture into California waters during El Niño. Both have been spotted recently. Lowe said a white shark nursery reappeared for the first time since 2011 in Santa Monica Bay, where juveniles frolic without bothering humans. Ludt said the aptly named longfin bigeye fish species was recorded for the first time in California this year when an angler caught one on the Venice Fishing Pier in Los Angeles. When two olive ridley sea turtle nests were found on a pair of Orange County beaches in September, they marked the first-ever recorded nest for any sea turtle species on the US West Coast, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The first was discovered by a beachgoer in Seal Beach on September 16, the second by lifeguards in neighboring Huntington Beach three days later, officials said. And other new species may yet arrive. "We still aren't fully through it," Ludt said. "It's still very much ongoing."

item.title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
item.description: Their relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices, a political headache for President Trump ahead of November's midterm elections
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Steve Holland, Daniel Flynn
item.content:encoded: From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel deal"] that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a bad week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington. Frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another [USN:L6N4620NO TEXT:"winter of Russian attacks"] on its energy infrastructure. Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an [USN:L8N4620FR TEXT:"unusually sharp"] series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks. The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow. Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia. Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said. 'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. "It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank. Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv. The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts. Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran , which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel. HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly [USN:L4N45Z20E TEXT:"Russian attack"] on the capital. Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters. Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off. Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"disrupted"] after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"an order originating from the White House"], Reuters reported on Thursday. The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration. That dependence gives Trump potential leverage as he pushes Kyiv toward negotiations with Moscow. Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"argue that"] Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow. Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy. “Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.”

item.title: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters
item.description: Redrawing congressional district lines splits neighbors and groups them with people far away.
item.dc:creator: Ally J. Levine, Bianca Flowers, David Hood-Nuño
item.content:encoded: It’s a political fault line that leaves neighbors on both sides with less say. 9th District5th District The street outside Tammy Jo O'Neal's home has become a political boundary with big implications. The city of Memphis used to sit almost entirely in one congressional district. The new map splits O'Neal from neighbors across the street, each now belonging to districts with voters halfway across the state who have different needs and interests. O'Neal sees the new map as more than a split block. “There's this divide that's happening in our lives,not just in our districts.” District 5 District 9 Tammy Jo O’Neal sits for a portrait on the front porch of their home on Elzey Ave in Memphis, Tennessee, US, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Seth Herald A citydivided By Bianca Flowers , David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine Published Oct. 17, 2026 6:00 a.m. EDT What happens when congressional district lines are redrawn, splitting neighbors and grouping them with people far away Four years before the Memphis redistricting, Republicans used a similar strategy in drawing new maps for Nashville. They split the city, which had voted overwhelmingly Democratic for roughly 70 years, into three broader districts where Republicans can now easily prevail. Battles over redistricting have long been intertwined with racism and political power, particularly in southern states like Tennessee. Sixty-four years ago, a federal court found Tennessee diluted voting power in urban areas where majority Black voters lived and ordered the legislature to redraw its congressional districts. For decades, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was a powerful tool for Black voters, particularly in the South, to challenge discrimination and protect political power among people of color to elect representatives who would advocate for their communities. The act significantly increased Black and Hispanic representation in Congress by curtailing certain redistricting practices, including splitting people of color among many districts or concentrating them in some districts to limit their impact in others. But those protections have been steadily weakened. In 2013, when Democrat Barack Obama was president, the Supreme Court’s decision on the Alabama case Shelby County v. Holder gutted a provision requiring federal approval before states change voting laws or political maps. In April, the court narrowed the Voting Rights Act further in Louisiana v. Callais , making it harder to challenge new maps that dilute the voting power of communities of color. The court essentially required such challenges to prove that districts were drawn intentionally to discriminate on the basis of race, and not for other reasons. Republicans argue their redistricting in Tennessee and elsewhere is about party politics, not race. They point out that Democrats regularly redraw districts in states they control to give their party easier election wins. Democrats have done the same in California, for example, said Steve Hickey, chair of the Republican Party in Williamson County, a popular suburban area south of Nashville. “This is part of a bigger game being played nationally, and I don’t think it’s fair to say that this was done to gut” the Voting Rights Act, he said. Redistricting in the United States is generally controlled by state legislatures, which adjust voter maps after the once-a-decade census. Both parties have historically used the process to help their candidates win future elections. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Texas launched an unusual mid-decade redistricting drive as part of a broader Republican push to gain congressional seats in half a dozen states, including Tennessee. Democrats responded with their own partisan redistricting in California and attempts that faltered in other states. Civil rights activists say Tennessee’s congressional districts, all of which currently favor Republicans, are now a testing ground for dismantling voting rights protections across the United States. “This lack of competition spills over and has racial implications,” said John Geer, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University who conducts polling in Tennessee. Reuters sought to quantify the impact of redistricting on the voters of Tennessee, examining public funding, demographics and socioeconomic factors to show why it’s important to residents when a city is split up like this. MemphisDistrict 9Suburbs of NashvilleDistrict 5District 8District 9 Population by race, one dot per person Black residents White residents Other races and ethnicities Memphis has the largest Black population in Tennessee. The city of some 630,000 people is 63% Black. Memphis accounted for 78% of the former District 9’s population, making it the only majority-Black district in the state. Earlier this year, the Tennessee legislature drew new district lines, splitting Memphis and its Black communities into three separate districts. The pieces of the city are now grouped with rural and suburban Tennesseans in districts that reach halfway across the state. Note: “White” and “Black” are non-Hispanic. “Other races and ethnicities” combines Hispanic or Latino residents of any race with the non-Hispanic categories Asian alone, American Indian and Alaska Native alone, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, Some Other Race alone, and Two or More Races. Sources: US Census Bureau (2020 census redistricting data; TIGER/Line boundaries); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads) Reuters spoke to more than 35 redistricting scholars, political analysts, civic leaders, political candidates and voters about the consequences of redistricting for the most vulnerable communities in Tennessee’s two biggest cities. Cities faced the biggest impact because rural areas were already represented by a Republican and continue to be so after the redistricting, albeit in districts with different demographics. Before redistricting, both Nashville and Memphis were overwhelmingly Democratic districts in an otherwise Republican state. In 2024, District 9, including most of Memphis, went 71% for Democrat Steve Cohen. In 2020, Jim Cooper, a Democrat, ran unopposed in Nashville’s District 5, winning more than 99% of votes cast. In 2022, the new District 5 flipped, with the Republican candidate winning 57%. Tennessee’s new maps have combined city, suburban and rural populations that have widely varying needs and political preferences. The residents of Nashville and Memphis, for instance, are far more likely to struggle with poverty, housing, public safety and related issues. Residents there could now struggle to elect Congress members who prioritize policies to address these issues, according to Odessa Kelly, executive director of Stand Up Nashville, a nonprofit community organization that advocates for racial and economic equality. She said Black voters in Nashville no longer felt they had someone to stand up for them in Congress, from federal funding going to the city to critical votes on bills that directly affect city residents. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed the Social Vulnerability Index to gauge how well a community can withstand and recover from an emergency, and to identify which communities may need the most support. Shelby County, home to Memphis, ranks among the most vulnerable of Tennessee’s 95 counties on various indicators such as housing cost burden and lack of access to a vehicle. Memphis, Nashville residents rank higher in social vulnerability A US government index compares Tennessee communities on socioeconomic and demographic factors gauging their resilience to unexpected hardships. 25th 50th 75th 100th percentile Lower vulnerability Higher vulnerability Shelby County (Memphis) Minority status Racial or ethnic minority 100 Davidson County (Nashville) Housing and transportation In structures of 10+ units 97 No vehicle available 94 More people than rooms 60 Lives in group quarters 56 Mobile homes 0 Household characteristics Aged 17 and under 97 Single-parent household 96 Speaks English less than well 91 With a disability 9 Aged 65 and over 5 Socioeconomic status Housing cost burdened 100 Unemployed 86 No health insurance 76 Below 150% of poverty 50 No high school diploma (25+) 16 0 Chart showing where Shelby County and Davidson County rank among Tennessee’s 95 counties on 16 measures of the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index, grouped into four themes, on a scale from the 0 to the 100th percentile with the other 93 counties as faint ticks. Both rank high on most measures — Shelby at the 100th percentile for racial or ethnic minority share and housing cost burden, Davidson at the 100th for apartments in large buildings and for people who speak English less than well. Both drop to the middle or bottom on poverty, the 50th percentile for Shelby and the 23rd for Davidson, and on residents aged 65 and over. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index 2022 In 2024, just over a third of Tennessee voters picked Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, and in 2020, Democrats won two congressional seats out of the state’s nine, carrying Nashville and Memphis. Now, every congressional district in Tennessee is considered “safe” for Republicans. Sandi Wells, a self-described “very conservative” voter from Williamson County, just outside Nashville, said it was “kind of odd” to group Memphis in the same district with parts of Williamson County 200 miles away. But she rejected the notion that districts should be drawn to protect Black voting power. “I don’t think we should have districts that are based on race,” she said. “I mean, that’s just ridiculous for anyone to even think that we should have that.” Shane Tinnin, a 52-year-old small business owner who maintains homes in both cities and has voted mostly for Democrats, understands that parties seek political power through redistricting but called the Memphis maps a particularly striking setback for Black political power. “In Nashville, it seemed really more like this is a political move,” he said, noting that it was not a Black-majority city. “When you do it in Memphis, where it’s an even more liberal district, but also a predominantly Black district, it just feels especially egregious to me.” Odessa Kelly, executive director at Stand Up Nashville, points to topics of focus for her and her team at a meeting in July. REUTERS/Seth Herald Volunteers for The Equity Alliance canvass through neighborhoods in Memphis to do “accountability” door knocks to speak with residents about elected officials following the GOP-led effort to redistrict the city. REUTERS/Seth Herald Securing funding Reuters examined how Nashville’s redistricting has impacted community project funding, under which lawmakers can seek federal money for local projects. Previously known as earmarks, community project funds returned to Congress with a more transparent process in fiscal year 2022 after a decade-long moratorium. A Reuters analysis found a dramatic shift in funding for Nashville after the city was split among three districts. Jim Cooper, a Democrat, steered most of the old 5th District’s project funding to Nashville in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. In the years since, only a small share of funding has gone toward projects in the city, including fiscal year 2027 requests still pending before Congress. Funding can vary greatly between representatives. Only John Rose, who currently represents the 6th District, has requested funding among the three members whose districts included Nashville after redistricting. Matt Van Epps and Andy Ogles have not pursued community project funding for their districts at all, arguing against such spending on principle. All three did not provide a comment or did not respond to a request to comment. Total Community Project Funding for districts that include Nashville After FY2023 FY2024 $18 mln $21 mln $2.5 mln Not Nashville $18 mln Nashville Nashville $3 mln $15.5 mln Before Two flow diagrams comparing Community Project Funds before and after redistricting.
