item.title: Central rivals Blues, Predators aim to keep building
item.description: Two teams looking to climb the Central Division standings will face off Saturday in Nashville, when the Predators host the St. Louis Blues.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Two teams looking to climb the Central Division standings will face off Saturday in Nashville, when the Predators host the St. Louis Blues. The Blues will wrap up a three-game road trip after they lost 5-4 to the Minnesota Wild on Thursday night. St. Louis scored twice in the final four minutes, including a short-handed goal by Robert Thomas, but coach Jim Montgomery's team could not complete the comeback to force overtime. "Well, 1-1 on a three-game road trip, we got to come out above .500," Montgomery said. "We'll get on the plane, get to Nashville, have a really good practice (Friday) and come out Saturday night with a little more determined effort than we had (Thursday)." Nashville, though, did force the extra session on Thursday. The Predators overcame a 2-0 deficit to San Jose midway through the third period and earned a point thanks to Steven Stamkos' last-second goal, which tied the contest. The Sharks prevailed in the shootout, extending Nashville's winless streak to three games (0-1-2). Nashville has leaned on its veterans, with all five of its leading scorers at least 32 years old. Stamkos, 36, leads the team with four goals and eight points. A two-time Stanley Cup winner with Tampa Bay, Stamkos is now in his third year with Nashville, which has only made the playoffs once in the last four seasons. "I think we're very well aware of where we want to be and how we want to begin the year," coach Andrew Brunette said. "So, I think we're putting a little bit added pressure on ourselves. For sure there's disappointment (with the overtime loss), but we just pick ourselves up and go back to work. You stacked a point out of it, and you build to the next game." Goalie Juuse Saros (2-2-2, 2.95 goals-against average), another Predators veteran, has started six of the team's seven games and stopped 30 shots in the loss to San Jose. The Finnish netminder has allowed just 18 of 187 shots, posting a .904 save percentage. Saros has faced the Blues 24 times over his 12 NHL seasons. He's 10-11-2 with a 3.36 GAA and an .885 save percentage. Nashville may get Mavrik Bourque back in the lineup. The 24-year-old center, acquired in July from the Dallas Stars, has missed the past week due to an upper-body injury, but he was on the ice for practice Friday. St. Louis had its two-game winning streak snapped Thursday, but the Blues have improved offensively, scoring 16 goals over their past three games. Mason McTavish, acquired from Anaheim in June, leads the Blues with five goals and eight points. The 23-year-old center has a five-game point streak, including three goals and an assist in his past two contests. Netminder Joel Hofer (2-2-1, 2.43 GAA) has started both games on the road trip. In eight career games against Nashville, Hofer, 26, is 4-3-0 with a 3.59 GAA and an .865 save percentage. Pavel Buchnevich, who had three assists in the 7-2 win over Ottawa on Tuesday, missed Thursday's game against the Wild due to the birth of his child. It's unclear whether he'll return for Saturday's game. --Field Level Media

item.title: Experts divided on whether Dodgers' sweep shifts MLB salary cap fight
item.description: Experts are divided over whether the Los Angeles Dodgers' sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series will affect Major League Baseball's labor talks, where owners are pushing for a salary cap that players oppose.
item.dc:creator: Rory Carroll
item.content:encoded: Experts are divided over whether the Los Angeles Dodgers' sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series will affect Major League Baseball's labor talks, where owners are pushing for a salary cap that players oppose. The big-spending Dodgers were thoroughly outplayed by the relentless Brewers, who rank 19th in payroll out of the league's 30 clubs. Milwaukee will return to the World Series for the first time in 44 years after vanquishing the two-time defending champions. Tony Torain, a partner at McDermott Will & Schulte who specializes in labor and employment law, said the result weakens the owners' case that there isn't enough parity in the sport. "I think we'll have a lockout and the league will still try to use that leverage," he said. "But in terms of making the argument for why they think they need a salary cap, the Brewers undercut it. There's definitely leverage on the PA's side," he said, referring to the players' association. He said the union will argue that player development, not payroll, drives winning. He also expects the union to press for higher minimum salaries, an idea it raised early in talks. In their first proposal in May, MLB owners asked for a hard cap of $245.3 million, including player benefits, and a payroll floor of $171.2 million, starting in 2027. The players have long opposed any form of salary cap. The current collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1. Torain said baseball's growing popularity puts added pressure on owners, who have never had a cap in the sport's history. The last time owners pushed for a cap, players went on strike in 1994. The 232-day stoppage forced the cancellation of that year's World Series. "If you have a lockout, it's not on TV, you can't go to the parks, so you're not getting those revenue sources," he said. MESSAGING WIN Bob Dorfman, a San Francisco-based sports marketing analyst, said the Dodgers' playoff exit will change little. "I don't think it's going to change anything that happens for those CBA talks," he said. At most, he said, the sweep is "a messaging win" for the union. He also questioned whether a cap would improve competitive balance, saying attendance, which has risen four seasons in a row, and viewership are strong without one. He agreed that a lockout is likely when the current agreement expires. He said he hopes a stoppage is short, but in a worst case the season could shrink to 70 to 80 games. He said he hopes owners will eventually put off the cap fight for a future contract negotiation. Dorfman said a lockout would anger fans and expects games to be lost, perhaps for a month or two in an optimistic scenario. He said owners tend to win labor fights because they can outlast unions. When reminded that owners failed to win a cap in 1994-95 season, he said, "I hope that happens again."

item.title: Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims
item.description: He made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech on Friday. "You know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it for years now. I've never been wrong." Mohammad is [USN:L5N3N60N8 TEXT:"one of the most common male names"] among Muslims, who often name their sons after the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam. Trump made the comment as he was discussing Iran during a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]. "Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, then pretended to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian has been president of Iran since 2024. The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response. Rights advocates and Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities. He has [USN:L1N45U12W TEXT:"escalated"] such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee. Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program. An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year [USN:L4N3ZU0AN TEXT:"attributed"] rising Islamophobia in the US in part to Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.

item.title: Missiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu
item.description: Missiles struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Missiles struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify the attackers. In Aden in southern Yemen, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-aligned Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility. No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said. Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely throttled by Iran since the US and Israel launched attacks on the country in February. With regional tensions and security threats raising concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies, Brent crude oil briefly touched [USN:L1N46201B TEXT:"$110 a barrel"] on Friday for the first time since May. Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued an alert early on Saturday for Abha in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border before sending an all-clear. Earlier they had issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month. Also early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes east of Yemen's northwestern city of Saada. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the area. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly. The Yemen conflict has become another front as the Iran war has widened into a regional conflict. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year. The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, [USN:L1N4610QE TEXT:"targeting"] [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"airports,"] oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital. A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

item.title: Nearly 12,000 California residents bought EVs using state rebate program
item.description: California said on Friday that nearly 12,000 residents bought electric vehicles since August using rebates under a new $270 million program funded by the state and automakers.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: California said on Friday that nearly 12,000 residents bought electric vehicles since August using rebates under a new $270 million program funded by the state and automakers. Still, overall EV sales have fallen in California and nationwide as President Donald Trump's administration has removed federal incentives for them. EV sales are up globally- fueled by rising oil prices. The program for California residents buying their first EV, which Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law in July, offers $3,500 rebates on new EVs with retail prices of up to $50,000 and a $1,750 rebate for used EVs costing no more than $25,000. California said EVs accounted for 18% of all sales in the state through September 30, down from 23% last year and 25% in 2024. Tesla (TSLA.O) vehicles account for more than half of EVs sold in California. About $70 million has been spent so far with 11,806 new EVs and 132 used EVs purchased — leaving $200 million in rebate funding. The vehicles purchased under the program include 5,658 Tesla, 1,700 Hyundai (005380.KS) , nearly 1,400 Toyota and 1,100 General Motors (GM.N) EVs. Nissan (7201.T) just joined the program and Mitsubishi Motors (7211.T) will begin in November, California said. Other automakers participating in the program are Ford (F.N) , Honda (7267.T) , Kia, Toyota's Lexus brand, Lucid, Rivian (RIVN.O) , Subaru (7270.T) and Volvo. There are no funds remaining for Tesla models under the program, which includes $135.5 million in state funding and $135.5 million from participating automakers. The federal government has dropped support for EVs and charging programs. Trump signed legislation in 2025 that killed the federal $7,500 EV tax credit and the federal $4,000 used-EV credit, which has reduced US sales. California's previous rebate program ended in 2023 and spent $1.49 billion to subsidize 586,000 EV purchases over a decade. Trump has taken aim at EVs on a number of fronts, including signing legislation in June 2025 against California rules, adopted by nearly a dozen other states, that aim to phase out new gasoline-powered cars by 2035. California has sued to challenge the procedure used to reverse the landmark EV rules. The administration has finalized other changes that will save automakers billions of dollars in purchasing credits from Tesla and others to meet prior regulatory requirements.

item.title: White House press secretary Zacharia fired in less than a week after facing criticism
item.description: The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger weeks before the midterms.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Trevor Hunnicutt, Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: White House press secretary [USN:FWN45V14O TEXT:"Katie Zacharia"] was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump 's top spokesperson. Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her [USN:L6N4601D0 TEXT:"legal credentials"] and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews. The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections , a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress. Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the job. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip. He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later. Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to succeed [USN:FWN4491F6 TEXT:"Karoline Leavitt"] a week ago. She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as an attorney. "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in an emailed statement on Wednesday. Reuters could not find records showing the Pepperdine University law school graduate was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia. During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she [USN:L1N46201S TEXT:"did not pass the bar"] exam. Law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar. Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about her firing. Earlier on Friday, she told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press. Trump hired Zacharia after expressing concerns about the media coverage of his administration, feeling he needed a new spokesperson who could amplify his achievements, according to two people familiar with the conversations. In a phone interview with Fox on Friday, Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary. Zacharia's quick exit meant she had what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any press secretary in the role's history. "Records are made to be broken," Anthony Scaramucci, who served as director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration, said on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

item.title: Teacher and armed parent teamed up to stop Oregon school shooter, police say
item.description: The 16-year-old shooter was stopped by a teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Bloom, Herbert Villarraga
item.content:encoded: A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday. Their actions on Thursday saved other lives, the local police chief told a press conference. A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said. TEACHER 'HELPED PREVENT MORE BLOODSHED,' POLICE SAY The unidentified teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before police arrived. This teacher, who was not injured, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press conference. "The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism," he said, without identifying her. Kenda Freeman told the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend the school, killed the shooter, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement. "He is not seeking recognition but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media. The shooting traumatized much of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, including 9-year-old fourth-grader Kalani Journeigh and her classmates, who heard the gunshots from a nearby classroom. "All of us were screaming and we were all, like, really scared," Kalani told Reuters, adding that she feared, "We might die." "My heart was beating really fast and after the couple of gunshots that we heard, it just stopped and we never heard it again," she said. A friend of hers was going to get therapy, she said, because "that was really traumatizing to her." Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a 16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him, police said. Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he obtained a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," the police chief said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." VICTIMS MOURNED Just before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle. The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived within three minutes of the first call, and the shooter was already dead, Krantz said. People in Bend gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow-crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene. "Thank God for that father," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears. "He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today." The family of the slain teacher, Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a "dream job" for her. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday's news conference. Lambert's family also praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude to him. "We think he is a hero," the family said, according to the statement. US school shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished in a school, or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a nonprofit online tracker. A separate online database, the Gun Violence Archive, has recorded 371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend incident, occurred in public schools, the archive said.

item.title: Chinese online retailer Temu agrees to data privacy curbs to settle Texas lawsuit
item.description: Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to settle data privacy claims raised by Texas and will restrict how it handles personal data from shoppers in the state, according to documents made public on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Jody Godoy, David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to settle data privacy claims raised by Texas and will restrict how it handles personal data from shoppers in the state, according to documents made public on Friday. Temu faces several lawsuits from US states concerned that the company unlawfully harvests US user data that could be accessed by the Chinese government. Texas is the first to resolve such claims. It is also the first time the company has agreed to keep personal data on US servers and restrict when it can be sent to China, Texas officials said. The company agreed to conduct annual independent product safety testing to identify products containing dangerous chemicals and materials. Temu must remove any products found to contain dangerous materials, terminate the seller and its affiliated stores, notify affected Texas consumers and issue full refunds. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said the settlement also requires Temu "to implement rigorous new product audits and safety standards to protect consumers from dangerous materials in products, including clothing and children’s items." He added it will prevent Temu from collecting and using Americans' data. Temu had more than 82.4 million active users in the United States as of September 2023, Paxton's office said. Temu will pay $3 million to the state as part of the settlement and Texas said failure to abide by various data security provisions would result in a potential $8 million penalty each year a violation occurs. Several states sued Temu in the wake of reports alleging Temu and parent company PDD Holdings < PDD.O > used invasive mechanisms in their apps. Temu, which did not admit wrongdoing, said in a statement the company "has come to an agreement to resolve this matter as we continue to focus on serving consumers and supporting businesses across Texas." Under the terms of the settlement, Temu agreed to restrict access to US data necessary to fulfill a transaction, such as shipping addresses, to China. Texas alleged that Temu used code that allows an inappropriate level of access to users’ devices. Temu has denied the allegations.

item.title: Thousands march in Albanian capital as anti-government protests spread
item.description: Thousands of young Albanians marched through Tirana on Friday, breaking some windows and traffic lights on the fourth day of an increasingly violent student-led campaign to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Thousands of young Albanians marched through Tirana on Friday, breaking some windows and traffic lights on the fourth day of an increasingly violent student-led campaign to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The demonstrations, which are spreading through the country, [USN:L1N4610AQ TEXT:"turned into a riot"] in the capital on Thursday, with protesters smashing windows, raiding a bank and clashing with police. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations that the students say the government ignored. "They are pushing us to the limits," said 19-year-old protester Enea, declining to give a second name for fear of arrest. He said his message to Rama was: "To resign as fast as possible before everything burns down." The students accuse officials of corruption and neglecting education and say they are angry about the sale of pristine parts of Albania's coast to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. The unrest is a challenge for Rama, who won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the European Union and is aiming for membership as early as 2028. "We will not bow to violence," he said on Facebook. BUSINESSES APPEAL TO PROTESTERS TO LEAVE THEM ALONE The students, many wearing masks, faced off against lines of riot police in front of the Education Ministry building. Some small businesses had their shutters down and notes on their facades saying: "We are with you. Do not damage our business all over the town." In the coastal town of Lezha, police clashed with stone-hurling protesters. Protests have also spread to Elbasan, Skhodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to garbage bins, local media reported. "We've been protesting peacefully for 140 days, and nothing was heard. So this is our only chance to be heard and get our rights that we deserve," a 19-year-old protester who gave her name only as Klea said. The demonstrations were sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was wrongfully sold for development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors for drug trafficking, charges his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. Political analyst Afrim Krasniqi said younger generations saw no future in Albania. "They see that all resources in the country, political resources, economic, everything is in the hands of oligarchs," he told Reuters. Corruption scandals have tarnised Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU. Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the accession process among Balkan countries. The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students [USN:L1N45Z0DG TEXT:"have staged weeks of protests"] and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.

item.title: Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
item.description: Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Le Poidevin
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 16 story has been corrected to say that the speaker was IOM's Arthur Erken, not Dejan Keserovic, in paragraphs 4 and 8.) Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday. With temperatures set to fall in the coming months, many families are struggling to secure reliable heating, electricity and water after years of war, the International Organization for Migration said. This week, Russian missiles and drones have [USN:L1N46209U TEXT:"rained down on Ukrainian cities"], amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv. "Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began," Arthur Erken, the IOM's regional director for Europe and Central Asia, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Kyiv. Nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced across Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while an estimated 3.8 million have returned after displacement, often to damaged or partially destroyed homes, according to the latest IOM figures. Ukrainians who returned to their homes within the last three months are the most likely to say they intend to leave again, reflecting growing concerns about deteriorating living conditions, the IOM said. European countries such as Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic currently host around 6 million Ukrainian refugees. Erken said he expected host countries to be preparing for more Ukrainians to leave if the situation got worse. Repeated Russian strikes on energy and other critical infrastructure have put increasing pressure on Ukraine's electricity, heating and water systems, while drone and missile attacks continue to kill and injure civilians across the country, the IOM said. Reliable access to water is emerging as a major concern because water systems depend heavily on electricity, the IOM said. The UN agency has installed 31 solar power stations to support water systems across Ukraine, but warned that needs remain immense. The IOM also warned that funding shortages could hamper aid efforts, with less than 7% of its 2026 Ukraine response plan funded so far, and said urgent resources were needed to improve insulation as households face freezing conditions.

item.title: Naftogaz chief says Ukraine's gas reserves hit six-year high ahead of winter
item.description: Ukrainian state oil and gas firm Naftogaz's acting CEO said the company has built its largest gas reserves in six years ahead of winter, despite a jump in Russian strikes on the company's facilities.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Polityuk
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian state oil and gas firm Naftogaz's acting CEO said the company has built its largest gas reserves in six years ahead of winter, despite a jump in Russian strikes on the company's facilities. Ukraine uses vast volumes of gas to heat its cities during the winter months, and the current season could be the most difficult of the nearly five-year war with Russia, which has sharply intensified its attacks on Ukraine's energy sector. The attacks also put at risk the colossal Soviet-era power stations which Ukrainian cities rely on for winter heat. Naftogaz CEO Sergii Fedorenko told Reuters Russia had attacked Naftogaz assets more than 400 times so far this year, twice as many times as in 2025. "This year, most of our facilities have come under attack," Fedorenko said, adding that oil and gas production, processing and transportation facilities, as well as thermal power plants in frontline regions, have been hit. "We are strengthening defences and digging in," he said. RESERVES AT 16 BILLION CUBIC METRES, NAFTOGAZ SAYS Fedorenko said Naftogaz had managed to bring the volume of reserves in underground storage facilities to 16 billion cubic metres, the highest since 2020. Ukraine began the previous heating season with reserves of less than 14 bcm. The government has said the country needed at least 13.2 bcm of gas in reserve to get through the winter. The rise in reserves comes as consumption has fallen this year, largely because Russian strikes on industrial infrastructure have already forced the shutdown of some factories. Fedorenko estimates that gas consumption in 2026 will fall to about 20 bcm from 21 bcm in 2025. He said it is difficult to make predictions during a war, when everything can change at any moment. "By the start of the heating season, we keep restoring and restoring our destroyed production," he said. "We look forward with caution. Every morning I wake up and check my phone to see if any of our facilities were hit overnight." Ukrainian legislation prohibits state-owned companies from disclosing data on the results of their operations in the energy sector. COLD WEATHER, RUSSIAN STRIKES DROVE IMPORTS TO A RECORD Ukraine is a net gas importer. Since 2015 it has stopped buying Russian gas directly, instead importing from European suppliers, primarily via Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary. Heavy frosts and Russian strikes on underground storage facilities forced Naftogaz to import a record 7.8 bcm of gas in 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, Fedorenko said. This season, it started buying gas early and has so far contracted more than 1 bcm of imports, 25% of which is LNG. "We contracted supplies specifically for the heating season, meaning we have contracts for delivery during a defined period — December through March," Fedorenko said. Ukraine operates Europe's largest underground gas storage facilities, with capacity of about 30 bcm, and Fedorenko said Kyiv has proposed that the EU store part of its gas reserves there, allocating one-third of the capacity for that purpose. Located more than 1 km underground, the gas is protected from attacks and can, if needed, be delivered very quickly to consumers, particularly in Eastern European countries, Fedorenko said. He said the Ukrainian gas storage tariff is currently the lowest in the EU.

item.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
item.description: Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Noel Randewich, Purvi Agarwal
item.content:encoded: Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend. The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise. [USN:L6N4620IB TEXT:"Nvidia-backed"] CoreWeave (CRWV.O) slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%. Broadcom (AVGO.O) fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index (.SOX) sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines. Investors on Friday were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries. "There is some fear in the market," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management in Seattle. "High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk." Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors [USN:L6N4611DN TEXT:"are weighing a lower valuation"] for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services (.SPLRCL) , down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology (.SPLRCT) . The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June. Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla (TSLA.O) , Meta Platforms (META.O) and Procter & Gamble (PG.N) . Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data. While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026. Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities. item.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
item.description: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson, John Geddie
item.content:encoded: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup. Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"reported"]. It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting. US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar. The US State Department declined to comment on Vance's presence in the delegation but said the bureau he heads was not playing a leading role on US policy toward Myanmar. The department's Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs is "shaping, implementing and engaging on" US policy toward the country, a spokesperson said, while Vance's Bureau of Intelligence and Research "informs policy makers but does not lead on policy." "The United States does not comment on the content and parameters of purported sensitive discussions," the spokesperson said, adding that the engagement with Myanmar "is rooted in the desire to achieve practical wins for the American people — particularly those impacted by transnational crime." A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges. Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going. A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said. Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres. US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role. The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country. "This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move. Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington [USN:S0N2TK07R TEXT:"declared a genocide"]. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says. The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank. "The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said. JAPAN'S ROLE UNCLEAR It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar. Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration. That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper. Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government. Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained. Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities. Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup. Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.

item.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
item.description: The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
item.dc:creator: Erin Banco, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service. Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"stopped working in Ukraine"] when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A person in Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). US PRESSURES UKRAINE OVER REFINERY ATTACKS The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party's prospects in the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"November midterm elections"]. But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran , which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: "No such request was ever made by the president." The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request. Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment. DECLINE IN RELATIONS Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv's continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop. The US delegation also explained Washington's decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"soften Moscow's stance"] on peace talks. That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict. In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal "weak." Trump called for elections in Ukraine and [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"Zelenskiy's ouster"]. Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was [USN:L1N45Z0GP TEXT:"still sharing intelligence"] with Ukraine. Following the move to restrict Ukraine's access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision. The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

item.title: Could hackers get inside my fridge?
item.description: An expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Lhomedet, Leo Marchandon
item.content:encoded: Hackers who [USN:L8N45Y11U TEXT:"sabotaged"] refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets exploited the growing connectivity of equipment that was once largely mechanical. From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals. CAN HACKERS REALLY GET INTO MY FRIDGE? In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked. In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device. In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network. WHAT HOUSEHOLD DEVICES COULD BE HACKED? The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems. Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected. Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data. The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical. WHAT COULD A HACKER ACTUALLY DO? Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device. A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network. Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls. In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts. COULD HACKERS TAKE OVER MY CAR, ELECTRICITY OR WATER SUPPLY? Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles. In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes. Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks. Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems. Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices. That does not mean they are immune from cyber attacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi‑Fi network. HOW CAN PEOPLE PROTECT THEIR DEVICES? Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available and regularly installing software updates. Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so. The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.
